Learning Objectives

MODULE 1 · FOUNDATION

Why This Training Exists

Right now, committees are operating in isolation. There is little cross-talk between committees, no consistent cross-training when leadership changes hands, and decisions are being made based on "what we did last time" rather than a shared understanding of the chapter's mission and current priorities.

This course gives every committee chairman a common structure — a charter, clear goals and objectives, and simple project management and Lean habits — so committees can operate independently without operating blind to each other.

Reflect

Think of one task your committee does "because that's how we've always done it." Do you actually know why it's done that way? Keep that example in mind — you'll use it in the first activity.

MODULE 1 · FOUNDATION

The Operating Model

Every committee's work should trace back to the chapter mission through a clear governance chain, then run on a repeating operating cycle.

Two parts, one system

Governance Chain — mission flows down: the Polemarch sets annual priorities, the Vice Polemarch translates them into committee charges, and the Committee Chairman builds the charter and runs the committee.

Operating Cycle — action flows back up: Charter → Project List → Budget Request → Yearly Calendar → Status Report, then the cycle refreshes. The five toolkit templates you'll see later map directly onto this cycle.

MODULE 1 · FOUNDATION

Chain of Ownership

Every level of the chain owns something specific. No overlap, no gaps.

1

Polemarch

Owns: chapter mission, vision & annual priorities.

2

Vice Polemarch

Owns: committee charters, cross-committee coordination, resource conflicts.

3

Committee Chairman

Owns: charter execution, goals & objectives, status reporting up the chain.

4

Vice Chairman

Owns: scheduling, mentor/member coordination, day-to-day logistics.

5

Committee Members

Owns: individual tasks on the Project List — one name per task, every time.

The Rule That Makes This Work: One Owner Per Task

Shared ownership is no ownership. At every level — chapter, committee, or individual task — exactly one name is accountable. If a box on the chart or a row on a list doesn't have exactly one owner, it isn't assigned yet.

MODULE 2 · TOOLS & PRACTICE

Project Management Essentials

Four simple habits, borrowed from Lean, that keep committees moving without adding bureaucracy. Click each one to learn more.

Visual Management
Shared lists & calendars
Standing Check-Ins
Define · Do · Review
Eliminate Duplicate Work
Reuse templates
RACI Matrix
Clarify roles
Visual Management
Keep the committee's Project List and the chapter's Yearly Calendar somewhere everyone can see, updated weekly. If a status only lives in one person's head or inbox, it isn't visible — and if it isn't visible, it isn't managed.
Standing Check-Ins (Plan → Do → Check → Act)
After every event, spend 10 minutes on what worked, what didn't, and what changes next time. Write it down so the next chair inherits it instead of relearning it the hard way.
Eliminate Duplicate Work
Don't rebuild a charter, budget form, or calendar from scratch every year. Copy last year's, update the dates and numbers, and reuse the tested format — that's what the toolkit templates are for.
RACI Matrix
For any activity that touches more than one role, write down who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed before you start — not after something falls through the cracks.
MODULE 2 · TOOLS & PRACTICE

Activity: 60-Second Sprint

⏰ 60-Second Sprint: Name Your Silo
PairsGroup size
2 minutesTotal time
IcebreakerPurpose
Instructions
  1. Turn to one person near you (or think of a real committee partner if working solo).
  2. You each get 60 seconds, one at a time, to name one recurring task your committee handles purely on precedent — something done a certain way just because "that's how we've always done it," without a clear owner or written reason.
  3. Your partner listens and asks one clarifying question: "Who actually owns that task right now?"
Intended Outcome
Makes the silo-and-precedent problem concrete and personal before the course explains the fix. Most people will struggle to name a clear single owner for their example — that gap is exactly what the Chain of Ownership and "one owner per task" rule are designed to close.
TOOLKIT · TEMPLATE 1

Committee Charter

The charter is the translation layer between "what the chapter is trying to do this year" and "what my committee does on Tuesday."

Goals vs. Objectives — the distinction that matters most

Goals are 2–3 broad, outcome-level statements: what does winning look like this year? Objectives are 3–5 SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) steps that ladder up to each goal.

Example

Goal: Strengthen college and career readiness among Kappa League participants.
Objective: By May, 80% of enrolled students complete a college/career readiness workshop.

TOOLKIT · TEMPLATE 2

Committee Project List

One running list per committee: task, owner, priority, status, due date. This is your Lean visual board.

  • One owner per task — every row needs exactly one name.
  • Status in three words — Not Started / In Progress / Blocked / Done. No paragraphs, no ambiguity.
  • Update it weekly and keep it visible to the whole committee, not just the chairman.
TOOLKIT · TEMPLATE 3

Budget Request

Every dollar requested should trace back to a specific charter goal or objective.

The form itemizes cost, funding source, and total, then ties the request to a charter objective in the Justification section — and routes for sign-off from the Committee Chairman, Vice Polemarch, and Polemarch/Treasurer.

TOOLKIT · TEMPLATE 4

Yearly Planning Calendar

One shared events timeline so committees stop discovering conflicts the week of an event.

Confirm real dates with the Vice Polemarch, then post the finished calendar on the chapter website so every committee — not just yours — can see it.

TOOLKIT · TEMPLATE 5

RACI Matrix

Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each committee activity.

A = Accountable R = Responsible C = Consulted I = Informed
Rule of Thumb

Exactly one A per row. If an activity has two Accountables or zero, it isn't actually owned yet — go fix it before moving on.

GUIDED PRACTICE

Activity: Build One Goal Live

📝 Build One Goal Live
Groups of 3–4Group size
5–7 minutesTotal time
Applied practicePurpose
Instructions
  1. Pick one sample committee: Scholarship, Guide Right/Kappa League, Social Action, or Black & White Ball/Fundraising.
  2. In 5 minutes, write one goal for that committee and two SMART objectives underneath it, using the Charter format from this course as a guide.
  3. Then list 3 tasks that would go on that committee's Project List for the next 30 days — include an owner and a due date for each, following the "one owner per task" rule.
Intended Outcome
Hands-on practice translating a broad committee purpose into a measurable goal-and-objective pair, then converting that into an actionable, individually-owned task list — the exact motion every chairman will repeat when writing their real charter.
MODULE 3 · BRINGING IT TOGETHER

Closing the Loop

Integrating committee operations with the chapter website turns a one-time training into lasting cross-committee visibility.

A planned Committee Resources section on the chapter website will host:

  • All five toolkit templates, downloadable any time.
  • Each committee's current charter and goals — so any chair can see what every other committee is working on.
  • The shared yearly planning calendar, so the whole chapter works off one timeline instead of five.
